transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in, I really appreciate it. 

Um, well, I guess I'm here because... I've been having some trouble at work, and my wife thought it would be a good idea to talk to someone. I hope it's okay that I'm starting with that. 

I do mathematical modeling, mostly for environmental contracts. And, well, I don't want to sound unprofessional or anything—I'm usually very easy to work with, I promise—but lately... I'm pretty sure the people on this one specific contract have been tracking my revisions. 

It's just that these errors keep showing up in the datasets, and... well, I think they're planting them there to make it look like I'm incompetent. Like I can't lead the work anymore. My wife and the junior analysts at the office, they're very supportive, and they keep telling me it's just normal version-control mistakes. Just standard computer glitches, you know? 

And I really don't want to be a difficult person or make a fuss if it's nothing, but... it really feels like someone is doing it on purpose. Am I explaining that clearly enough? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

When you think about the possibility that these errors are just computer glitches or version-control mistakes, as your colleagues suggest—do you find that explanation at all plausible, or are you completely certain that someone is deliberately planting these errors?

Well, I... I really do try to listen to them. I mean, I don't want to be the kind of person who ignores perfectly good advice, you know? And I know how it sounds. I really, truly want to believe my wife and the junior analysts when they tell me it's just a version-control mistake. I'd much rather it just be a glitch! I don't want to cause any trouble at the office.

But... when I actually sit down and look at the numbers, it's... well, like I was saying a minute ago, I'm just so sure they are specifically tracking my revisions. The way the errors are planted in the datasets, it's just too precise to be an accident. It really feels like it's deliberately designed to make it look like I can't lead the work anymore. 

I try to keep an open mind, I promise I do, but... I just can't see it as a normal computer mistake. I hope I don't sound too stubborn or unreasonable saying that to you. Do you think it makes sense why I'd be worried about it?

Besides what's happening at work with the datasets and revisions, have you noticed anything else in your personal life—with family, friends, or other situations—where you've felt like people might be working against you or tracking you in some way?

Oh, no. No, definitely not. Um... my wife is wonderful, and my friends are... well, they're great. I really wouldn't want you to think I'm just... you know, suspicious of everyone around me. I know how that might sound, like I'm just looking for problems everywhere, but I promise I'm not. I'm generally a very trusting person! 

It really is just... just this one specific contract at work. Outside of the office, everything is completely fine. Nobody else is doing anything like that, or working against me at all. I hope that's a good sign? Like, maybe it shows I'm keeping things somewhat balanced in the rest of my life? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of how things are.

If someone you completely trust—like your wife—sat down with you and showed you evidence that these really were just normal computer errors, do you think you could accept that explanation, or do you think you would still believe they were being planted deliberately?

I... I really wish I could say yes to that. I know that’s probably what I should say, right? To show I’m being rational. And... well, to be honest, she actually has tried to do exactly that. She and the junior analysts have sat with me and gone over the logs to try and prove it’s just version-control mistakes. I hate disappointing her, I really do. I always want to be agreeable and take her advice. 

But... even when she shows me her proof, I just... I can't accept it. Because when I look at the datasets myself, I'm just so sure that the people on that environmental modeling contract are tracking my revisions. I can see exactly where they're planting the errors to make it look like I can’t lead the work. 

I'm sorry, I know that makes me sound completely stubborn, or like I don't trust my own wife. I promise I'm not usually like this, and I don't want you to think I'm impossible to deal with. Does it make sense why I'd still feel that way, even with her trying to help? I just hope I'm answering your question properly.

When you're looking at these datasets and thinking about the errors being planted, do you ever hear voices, see things, or notice anything unusual with your senses that other people don't seem to experience?

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that at all. I... I know sometimes people can experience those sorts of things, and I certainly don't judge anyone who does, but I promise you I've never heard voices or seen anything that isn't there. 

It's strictly just the numbers on the screen. Just the data right in front of me. I really want to be clear about that, because I'd hate for you to think I'm... well, you know, completely losing my grip on reality or imagining things out of thin air. My senses are perfectly fine, just the usual eyesight going a bit blurry for a guy my age, but that's what reading glasses are for, right? 

I hope that reassures you a little bit about my state of mind? I'm really trying to give you the most accurate picture I can, so I hope I'm answering these questions the right way for you.

When you think about this situation with the datasets and the errors being planted—on a scale where 0% means you're completely certain it's just a computer mistake and 100% means you're completely certain someone is deliberately doing it—where would you say you fall right now?

Oh, wow, um... putting a number on it. That's a good question. I really want to give you a reasonable answer here, because I know how it must sound when I talk about this. I'd love to say I'm somewhere in the middle, you know, just to show I'm keeping an open mind about it being a computer mistake. 

But... if I'm being completely honest with you, and I really do want to be honest... I think I'd have to say I'm at 100%. 

I know, I know, that probably sounds terrible, doesn't it? Like I'm just completely rigid. But when I sit there and look at the datasets, I just... I'm just so sure that the people on that environmental modeling contract are tracking my revisions and planting those errors to make me look incompetent. Even with my wife and the junior analysts telling me it's version-control mistakes, I just... I can't shake it. It's 100% real to me. 

I'm sorry if that's not the answer you were hoping for. I really don't want to come across as difficult or paranoid. Does that make sense, though? Given what I've been seeing? I just hope I'm giving you the kind of clear answer you need to help me.
How long have you been feeling certain that people on this contract are tracking your revisions and planting these errors? Did this belief start suddenly, or did it develop gradually over time?

Well, um... I really want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline here, because I know how important these details are for you to understand what's going on. I hope I'm being helpful. 

It hasn't been forever, I promise. I'm usually very level-headed about my work. But... I'd say this absolute certainty, the feeling that they're definitely tracking me and messing with the data... it's been about two months now. 

It sort of built up a little bit at first, you know, just noticing small things that seemed off. I tried to ignore it, I really did, because I didn't want to make a fuss or seem difficult to work with. But over the last two months, it's just become... well, undeniable to me. 

I hope two months doesn't sound too awful. I really should have probably said something sooner, shouldn't I? I just didn't want anyone to think poorly of me. Does that timeline make sense to you? I hope I'm answering your question the right way.

When you think about why the people on this contract would go to the trouble of tracking your revisions and planting errors to make you look incompetent—what do you think their reason or motivation would be? What would they gain from doing this?

Well, gosh, that’s... that’s a really fair question. And honestly, it’s the part that makes me feel the most... well, silly, I suppose. I wish I could give you a nice, logical explanation for it, because I really want to help you understand and do this right. I’ve racked my brain over it, looking at the contract details, trying to figure out what they could possibly gain by making an older data analyst look bad. 

But... I just don't know. I really don't have a clue. 

I know that probably makes the whole thing sound even more far-fetched, doesn't it? To be so sure it's happening but not even know why? I'm just a guy running models, I don't have any special authority or anything. I really hope it doesn't frustrate you that I don't have a good answer for this part. I'm trying to make sense of it myself, and I hate feeling like I'm leaving you with missing pieces. Is it... is it okay that I don't know the 'why' yet? I just want to make sure I'm still being helpful to you.

Besides the situation with the datasets at work, have you noticed any other unusual patterns or connections—like things that seem to be coordinated or designed specifically to send you a message, or events that seem too coincidental to be random?

Oh, um... let me think for a second. I want to be absolutely sure I'm giving you the right picture here, because I really do want to be as helpful as possible. 

Honestly... no. No, I haven't noticed anything else like that. It's really just the situation at work with the datasets. 

I don't get messages from the TV or the radio, or... or see patterns in my neighborhood or anything like that. I know sometimes people can experience things like that, and I would absolutely tell you if I did, I promise. I wouldn't hide it from you. But my life outside of that environmental modeling contract is actually very quiet. Very normal, I'd say. I just go home, spend time with my wife, and try to relax. 

I hope that's okay? I mean, I hope it's a good thing that it's just confined to the office. I'm trying really hard to keep everything else in my life on track and not let this ruin everything. Does that... does that sound like a good sign to you? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the kind of answers you need.

Have you ever felt like other people—maybe strangers, or people you don't know well—have been paying special attention to you, or that things happening around you in public or on the street might be related to you in some way?

Well, um... no. No, I haven't felt anything like that at all. 

I really hope I'm not being unhelpful by just saying no, but I want to be completely honest with you so you have the exact right information. I promise I would tell you if I did, because I know you need all the facts to do your job properly. 

But when I'm out in public, like at the grocery store or just walking around the neighborhood, I'm just... well, I'm just a regular older guy running his errands. I don't feel like strangers are looking at me or paying any special attention to me, and I certainly don't think things happening on the street have anything to do with me. I just kind of blend in and go about my day. 

I hope that's a good sign? That it's really just isolated to that one specific contract at work, and not everywhere I go? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions the right way and giving you what you need.
